title: 21 Annoying Student Behaviors That Are Indeed Enforceable
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Responding to a frequently asked question, Linsin compiles a list of 21 minor, seemingly petty behaviors — humming, sighing, muttering, cutting in line, hand-waving to get attention, and similar — that he says are legitimately enforceable as rule violations rather than things to overlook. His central claim is that these behaviors matter because they disrupt learning, invite further misbehavior, and erode a broader culture of excellence, even though none of them individually seem serious. He argues that a well-taught classroom management plan doesn't need to name every specific instance explicitly — if students understand the plan in enough detail, something like kicking a classmate in line is self-evidently a violation without further explanation. The real diagnostic question he poses isn't whether students understand what breaks the rules, but whether the teacher does: consistent enforcement is only possible if a teacher can instantly and confidently judge whether a given behavior crosses the line. The list functions as a calibration tool for teachers unsure where to draw enforcement boundaries.
points: All 21 listed behaviors, though individually minor, are framed as enforceable because they disrupt learning or break a core rule.
A well-taught plan doesn't need every specific behavior spelled out — clear, detailed modeling should make violations self-evident.
The list explicitly isn't exhaustive; it reflects the behaviors teachers most often ask Linsin about at talks and in coaching.
The real diagnostic isn't whether students know the boundaries, but whether the teacher can judge a violation without hesitation.
quotes: Teachers ask me frequently if minor but annoying student behaviors are enforceable.
Although SCM allows you to create the exact classroom you want, personally I would enforce a consequence in response to every behavior on the list.
Your students must know what is and isn’t okay so well that all 21 are obvious. Even if each one isn’t expressly stated.
For example, kicking a classmate in line isn’t something you have to define as against the rules. It clearly is. No explanation is needed.
A bigger concern than whether students know what types and categories of behaviors are unacceptable is whether you do.
